agent_notes: The superscription 'of David' is verse 1 here (KJV 37:0, 37:1 share the Hebrew verse). The psalm is an alphabetic acrostic, loosely: אל (1), בטח (3), גול (5), דום (7), הרף (8), ועוד (10), זומם (12). I mention it once, here, as my own observation; no commentary in the packet says so.

תִּתְחַר: Rashi, Radak and Meiri read it as a verb of 'contending/mixing in' (cf. Jer 12:5, 'how will you compete with horses'); Ibn Ezra, Meiri and Malbim also allow the root חרה 'to burn, be angry'. STEPBible's 'fret' follows the second. I kept 'fret' in the literal layer, which keeps the burning image, and gave both options in the note.

ארץ is 'land' throughout vv. 3, 9, 11 (the KJV varies between 'land' in v3 and 'earth' in vv. 9 and 11). I used 'land' everywhere in the literal layer. The echo in Matthew 5:5 reads the verse with 'earth'; I note it in the commentary but do not import it.

Meiri on 'gnashing' as scoffing/mockery and Ibn Ezra on 'gnashing in anticipation of the grab' are interpretive extensions; I cite them as what they are, and rely on the plain sense (teeth grinding in malice) for the dramatic layer.

agent_notes: אֶזְרָח is the hard word. The KJV 'green bay tree' comes from the older versions' 'cedar' tradition and is not in the Hebrew. I glossed it 'native' (as in Lev 24:16) and put '[tree]' in brackets in the literal layer, following Metzudat Zion; Ibn Ezra and Meiri read it as a person with a large family, and Rashi as one rooted in the land with possessions. The five English versions split three ways and I chose the plainest Hebrew sense. מִתְעָרֶה is also uncertain: 'spreading himself' (KJV, YLT) versus 'rooted' (Rashi, Metzudat Zion); I gloss it 'baring/spreading himself' and mention both.

The Masoretic text reads וַיַּעֲבֹר 'and he passed', in the third person, while the next clause switches to 'I sought him'. I believe the Septuagint and some other ancient versions read the first verb as first person ('and I passed by'), which would make the speaker the one who goes past and finds the tree gone; I have not checked this against the manuscripts, so it is stated only in my own words with no source. The translation follows the Hebrew as pointed.

agent_notes: The perfect נִשְׁמְדוּ and נִכְרְתָה are rendered as prophetic perfects ('are destroyed', 'is cut off'); YLT puts them in the past, KJV in the future. The Hebrew form allows both, and the sentence is a general truth. I kept the English present-perfect in the literal layer and flagged it.
The STEPBible gloss for עַל is 'on'; KJV and ASV have 'in'. I kept 'upon' in the literal layer because Rashi and Metzudat David read על as 'upon the support (מִשְׁעֶנֶת) of the LORD'.

The Hebrew has both וַיְפַלְּטֵם (wayyiqtol) and יְפַלְּטֵם (yiqtol) side by side. The doubling is in the text as pointed; Radak reads it as emphasis on the abundance of help. I translate both and keep them visible. STEPBible glosses the second as 'he delivers them'; I made the sequence 'delivered ... delivers' to show the shift of tense.
STEPBible glosses חָסוּ 'they have taken refuge'; I gloss it 'they took refuge' to match the narrative past of the verse. The root חסה is the shelter image, which KJV 'trust' flattens.

וְהִתְחוֹלֵל: the commentators split between 'wait longingly' (from יחל/תוחלת: Rashi, Radak, Meiri, Metzudat) and 'writhe, as a woman in labour' (from חיל: Ibn Ezra's preferred reading, also Radak's alternative). The literal layer takes 'wait longingly'; the 'writhe' reading appears only in the gloss and the commentary.
STEPBible glosses דּוֹם 'be still' and the five English versions say 'rest'/'be silent'. Root דמם is silence first (cf. Lev 10:3 as Rashi cites it), so I translate 'be silent' and keep 'rest' out.

notes.note: Commentators on this window are cited by name and verse as they appear in the packet; Psalm 37 is an alphabetic acrostic and several verses here open with successive letters (v. 25 nun, v. 27 samekh, v. 30 pe, v. 32 tsade, v. 34 qof, v. 35 resh). I mention the acrostic only where it explains the compressed, proverb-like style.
